q: Fodor argues his a priori conditions on propositional attitudes (PAs) demand treating them as:
a: Relations between organisms and internal representations
e: This converges with what cognitive psychologists arrived at independently, which he takes as a reason to think it's true.

q: Condition I says PAs should be analyzed as relations. What's the only known alternative, which Fodor calls hopeless?
a: The 'fusion' view: 'believes-it's-raining' is a single unstructured predicate
e: On fusion, 'John believes it's raining' is atomic, like 'John is purple'. 'Talk about counter-intuitive!'

q: Which is one of Fodor's objections to the fusion view?
a: There are infinitely many 'a believes ___' sentences, so if each were atomic, how could English be learned?
e: Davidson's learnability point. Also: on fusion, it's an accident that 'it will rain' appears in both 'fears' and 'believes' sentences.

q: 'Vendler's Condition' requires a theory of PAs to explain:
a: The parallelism between verbs of propositional attitude and verbs of saying
e: What we can believe/hope/doubt are the very things we can assert/inquire/demand.

q: 'Frege's Condition' requires a theory of PAs to account for their:
a: Opacity: substitution of identicals and existential generalization can fail inside belief contexts
e: Fodor notes fusion does satisfy this one, which shows Frege's condition alone under-constrains a theory.

q: 'Aristotle's Condition' says the objects of PAs have logical form. The paradigm example is:
a: The practical syllogism (John believes washing his car will make it rain, wants rain, so washes his car)
e: Mental states interact causally in virtue of their content, and the generalizations refer to their form.

q: Answering 'if John believes P & Q, P & Q is inferentially inert', Fodor distinguishes:
a: What's entailed by what's believed vs. what's entailed by believing it
e: P & Q always entails P. It's 'John believes P & Q' that isn't subject to simplification of conjunction.

q: Condition V requires a theory of PAs to:
a: Mesh with empirical accounts of mental processes (e.g., 'cost accounting' of complexity)
w: Avoid all reference to the brain
e: Analogy: 'water is H2O' must, with empirical premises, explain water's properties.

q: Carnap's theory construes PAs as relations between people and:
a: Natural-language sentences they're disposed to utter
e: It handles conditions I–V surprisingly well, but runs into objections 1–7.

q: Brown and Lenneberg's 'codability' experiments found that:
a: Colors with simpler English descriptions were easier to recognize and recall
w: Language plays no role in memory
e: This fits Carnap: what you (opaquely) remember is the description.

q: Which is the easiest objection to Carnap to fix, per Fodor?
a: His account of the belief relation is behavioristic (dispositions to utter)
e: The fix is to turn functionalist: a token of 'it's raining' plays a certain causal role.

q: The Dani findings are 'a shock' for Carnap's theory because:
a: English codability predicted recall for Dani speakers, whose language has no chromatic color vocabulary
w: Dani speakers had perfect color memory
Dani speakers couldn't recall any colors
e: How could English sentences be objects of a monolingual Dani's attitudes?

q: Objection 7 against Carnap is circularity about:
a: First-language learning, which itself requires beliefs, hypotheses and expectations
e: So some PAs must not be relations to natural-language sentences.

q: Fodor's solution keeps which part of Carnap's theory and drops which part?
a: Keeps: objects of PAs are sentences. Drops: they're NATURAL-language sentences.
e: Objects of PAs are formulae in an Internal Representational System, a language of thought.

q: Fodor assumes the internal representational system is:
a: Innate and universal (to the extent an organism shares our mental processes)
e: That would explain the Dani data and language learning. If Whorf-Sapir turned out true, the theory could fail.

q: What does Fodor's 'they are flying planes' example show?
a: Psycholinguistics needs a grammar that speakers internally represent, so internal representations are required anyway
e: Why the grammar and not some 'schmamar'? Only because G-proper is the system speakers actually use to represent sentences.

q: Why won't Fodor just say 'PAs are relations to propositions. Punkt!'?
a: Propositions lack form (bad for computation), and he can't see how organisms relate to them except via internal formulae
e: Propositions can be MEDIATE objects of PAs, with internal representations doing the mediating.

q: Fodor says if the representational theory of mind is true, the main remaining problem for philosophy of mind is:
a: What relates internal representations to the world (their semantic interpretation)
e: 'Psychology is all the philosophy of mind that we are likely to get.'
